summary: ModStableSwap is a faithful two-coin port of Curve's StableSwap: getD/getY reproduce the reference Newton iterations (verified numerically to ~1e-28 against a high-precision solver across A in [1,10000] and skews to 1e8:1, with no underflow found in a 3,000-case sweep), balances are normalised to 18 decimals, first-LP share inflation is blocked by internal accounting, removeLiquidity is proportional, and the owner cannot touch principal (only A, fees and the sink). As a swap venue for a genuinely 1:1 pair of plain ERC20s it works and its LPs' principal is not at risk from any finding here. The worst thing found is what the catalog offers on its `oracle` port: price() is a fee-inclusive spot read that a flash loan moves from 1.0 to 5,495 (5x depth) or to 0.0025 (2x depth) for a few bps of round-trip cost, returns 0 on an empty pool, and collapses when the pool is shallower than one whole coin - wired to ModCDP/ModLendingPool/ModPerps/ModBonding that is a one-transaction drain of the consumer or a bricked liquidation path, hence the critical. Four medium issues sit in the pool's own economics: no reentrancy guard with pull-before-account ordering (LP theft if a hook-bearing token is wired), instant A changes with no ramp (a 200->1 step on a 1.3M/0.7M pool reprices coin0 by 27% and drops virtualPrice 2.3% into an arbitrageur's pocket), no imbalance fee on deposits (add-then-remove is a swap that beats exchange() and pays zero fee), no rate provider (the docs' own suggested LST/asset pairing bleeds the staking yield to arbitrage since the catalog's lst block is share-based), and no reconciliation for fee-on-transfer/rebasing tokens. Deploy it as a market for plain, truly-at-par tokens behind a governor/timelock, with slippage set client-side; do not wire its price() into anything that lends or mints.

findings.title: price() is a fee-inclusive spot read that a flash loan moves by orders of magnitude; wired to the CDP/lending/perps/bonding oracle ports it is a one-transaction drain
findings.where: price() L120-L123, getDy() L107-L117; consumers cdp.sol L78 collateralValue() and L161 liquidate(), lending.sol L61 and L129, perps/bonding oracle ports
findings.detail: The catalog advertises this block as `provides: oracle` and price() is exactly what a canvas edge to ModCDP/ModLendingPool/ModPerps/ModBonding reads. It is computed from the current storage balances with no TWAP, no observation window and no bound: whoever moves the pool last in a block sets the number every consumer will read. A stable pool feels manipulation-resistant only near par; past the amplified region it is a constant-product tail. Simulated on a 1M/1M pool at A=200, fee 4 bps: pushing 1x the pool depth of coin1 in prints price(coin0)=2.04; 5x prints 5495; 10x prints 18107. Pushing coin0 in prints 0.489 at 1x and 0.0025 at 2x. The round trip through a stableswap costs only fees plus curvature (a few bps on the notional), so the attacker's capital is a ModFlashLender or any flash source, not their own. Three more defects make it worse as a feed: (a) dy is net of feeBps so the price is biased low by the fee even when untouched; (b) getDy returns (0,0) when either balance is 0, so an empty pool reports price 0 - ModCDP.liquidate() and ModLendingPool then divide by zero (liquidations bricked) and collateralValue() is 0 for everyone; (c) it quotes ONE WHOLE coin0 (10**decimals), so once the pool is shallower than one coin the quote collapses (a 1e6/1e6-wei pool reports ~1e-12), which in a CDP makes every position liquidatable and lets a keeper repay dust and seize the full collateral because seize is capped at p.collateral. None of this harms the pool's own LPs; the loss lands in whichever block trusts the number.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy ModStableSwap(USDC, MODUSD) with LPs at 1M/1M, ModCDP with collateral=USDC and oracle=stableswap (the canvas suggests this edge), and a ModFlashLender over MODUSD (or use any external flash source). 2. In one tx: flashLoan 5M MODUSD; exchange(false, 5M) into the pool - pool is now ~408 USDC / 6M MODUSD and price() returns ~5495e18. 3. Deposit 1,000 USDC into the CDP: collateralValue() = 5.49M; borrow at minCollateralRatio 150% -> mint ~3.6M MODUSD. 4. exchange(true, ...) the pool back toward par to recover the MODUSD (round trip cost ~8 bps of 5M plus curvature), repay the flash loan. 5. Walk away with ~3.6M freshly minted stablecoin against 1,000 USDC; the CDP is insolvent and the debt is never repaid. Variant (DoS/seizure): drain the pool with removeLiquidity or let it sit below one whole coin0; price() -> ~0; every CDP position is under-collateralised; liquidate(user, 1 wei) seizes p.collateral in full.
findings.recommendation: Do not expose spot as `oracle`. Either drop `oracle` from `provides`, or add a TWAP (cumulative price per block with a configurable window, EMA of the last-block price like Curve's `price_oracle`), refuse to quote when depth is below a minimum (revert, never return 0), quote the mid without the fee, and document which way round the quote is (coin0 in coin1). Consumers should be wired to ModFixedOracle or an external feed; if a pool price must be used, wrap it in a bounded, lagging oracle and add sanity bands in the consumer (max deviation per block).

findings.title: No reentrancy guard and pull-before-account ordering: a token with transfer hooks lets a depositor mint shares for the same D growth twice, and lets a trader chain stale-quoted swaps
findings.where: addLiquidity() L132-L143 (d0 read at L133, pull at L135-L136, balances written at L137-L138), exchange() L167-L181 (quote at L167, pull at L171/L177, balances at L172-L173/L178-L179)
findings.detail: addLiquidity snapshots d0 before the external transferFrom calls and only updates balance0/balance1 afterwards. If coin0 or coin1 can call back into the sender during transferFrom (ERC777 tokensToSend, ERC1363, any token with hooks), the sender can re-enter addLiquidity or exchange while the outer call's d0 is stale. The inner deposit is minted normally; when the outer call resumes it computes shares from (d1 - d0) where d1 now includes the inner deposit too, so that growth is paid twice. Simulated on a 1000/1000 pool at A=200: outer deposit 100 with an inner deposit 500 during the pull hook yields 1249 shares for 600 deposited, worth ~1000 of the 2600 in the pool - ~400 taken from existing LPs in one call, and nesting deeper takes more. exchange() has the sibling problem: amountOut is fixed at L167 before the pull, so nested exchanges are all quoted against the same pre-trade balances and the curve's slippage is never applied between them; the subtraction at L173/L179 only stops the final total from exceeding the balance. No catalog token has hooks, so this is dormant unless an external hook-bearing token is wired as coin0/coin1 - with such a token it is a direct LP theft and should be read as high.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy the pool over an ERC777-style stable (attacker-controlled contract as the sender so tokensToSend fires). 2. Honest LPs seed 1000/1000. 3. Attacker calls addLiquidity(100, 0, 0). 4. Inside the tokensToSend hook triggered by coin0.pull, attacker calls addLiquidity(500, 0, 0): d0=2000 (balances untouched yet), shares = 1000*(2499-2000)/2000 = 249 minted. 5. Outer resumes: balance0 += 100, d1 = getD(1600,1000) ~= 2599, shares = 1249*(2599-2000)/2000 ~= 374 more. Attacker holds 623 of 1623 shares (38%) for 600 of 2600 in assets (23%). 6. removeLiquidity(all) walks away with ~1000 of assets.
findings.recommendation: Add a nonReentrant modifier to addLiquidity, removeLiquidity, exchange and collectAdminFees. Additionally re-read balances after the pulls (or pull first, then compute d0 from balances before adding the new amounts) so a stale d0 cannot be used, and consider measuring received amounts via balanceOf deltas (which also addresses STABLESWAP-6).

findings.title: setParams() changes A instantly with no ramp; on a skewed pool that is a step change in every price and in virtualPrice that the owner or any mempool watcher can arbitrage out of LPs
findings.where: setParams() L202-L208; getD() L75, getY() L87, virtualPrice() L101-L105
findings.detail: Curve ramps A linearly over at least a day precisely because the invariant, and therefore the marginal price of a skewed pool, is a function of A. Here the owner writes `amp` in one call, anywhere in [1, 10000]. Simulated on a 1.3M/0.7M pool at 4 bps: A=200 quotes coin0 at 0.9960 and D=1,999,508; A=1 quotes 0.7256 and D=1,953,128. The 2.3% fall in D is a 2.3% fall in virtualPrice - the number the docs promise 'only ever goes up' and the number any LP-accounting consumer trusts - and the 27% price step is free money for whoever trades across the change. The owner can bracket their own transaction; anyone else can sandwich the public setParams tx in the mempool. Raising A on a skewed pool has the mirror effect. Because the pool's fee is at most 100 bps, nothing in the design absorbs a step of this size.
findings.exploit: 1. Pool is 1.3M coin0 / 0.7M coin1, A=200 (skew is normal for a stable pool after a directional flow). 2. Owner submits setParams(1, 4, 5000), or a bot sees it pending. 3. Front-run: exchange(true, 300k) coin0 -> coin1 at ~0.996, receiving ~298.8k coin1 and skewing the pool further. 4. setParams lands; A=1 reprices coin0 at ~0.73 (coin1 at ~1.38). 5. Back-run: exchange(false, 298.8k) coin1 -> coin0, receiving far more coin0 than was paid in step 3. The gain is paid by LPs via the lower D; virtualPrice steps down 2.3% and the pool is left further from par.
findings.recommendation: Implement rampA(futureA, futureTime) / stopRamp with a minimum ramp duration (Curve: 1 day) and a bounded per-ramp change (e.g. at most 10x), and read the interpolated A in getD/getY. Gate setParams behind the timelock/governor port so the change is public well ahead of execution. Keep feeBps/adminFeeBps changes separate from A.

findings.title: addLiquidity charges no imbalance fee, so a one-sided deposit plus a proportional withdrawal is a swap that pays zero fee and beats exchange()
findings.where: addLiquidity() L127-L147 (share formula L143), removeLiquidity() L150-L160, getDy() fee L114
findings.detail: Shares are minted for the full D growth of any deposit, balanced or not. Curve charges fee*N/(4*(N-1)) on the imbalanced part of a deposit and of a withdrawal because otherwise liquidity operations become a fee-free swap path. Simulated on a 1M/1M pool at A=200, fee 4 bps: addLiquidity(100k, 0) then removeLiquidity(all shares) returns 52,375 coin0 + 47,614 coin1, i.e. 47,625 coin0 was converted to 47,614 coin1 at 0.99976 - while exchange(true, 47,625) returns 47,595 at 0.99936, 19 coin1 of which is fee. The deposit route is strictly better for the trader (curve slippage on the one-sided deposit is smaller than the fee at this A), so any router or arbitrageur will use it and LPs and the admin fee sink collect nothing from that flow. When the pool is skewed the effect compounds: depositing the scarce coin earns a premium in shares, then a proportional withdrawal realises it at zero fee. No principal is lost, but the pool's only revenue is optional for informed traders, and volume that should nudge the pool toward par via fees does not.
findings.exploit: 1. Pool 1M/1M, A=200, fee 4 bps. 2. Trader wanting coin1 for coin0 calls addLiquidity(100_000e18, 0, minShares) - receives ~49,986e18 shares. 3. Same tx: removeLiquidity(shares) - receives 52,375 coin0 and 47,614 coin1. 4. Net: 47,625 coin0 -> 47,614 coin1 with no fee taken; exchange() would have paid 19 coin1 in fees and received 47,595. Repeat for any size; the advantage over exchange() grows with the fee setting.
findings.recommendation: Apply Curve's imbalance fee in addLiquidity: compute the ideal balanced amounts for the new D, charge `feeBps * N / (4 * (N - 1))` on |actual - ideal| per coin (crediting adminFeeBps of it to adminBalance), and mint shares from the D computed on the fee-adjusted balances. If a one-coin withdrawal is ever added, apply the same fee there. Alternatively, require deposits to be within a tolerance of the pool ratio.

findings.title: rate0/rate1 are decimal scalers only: pairing a share-based LST (the catalog's own ModLiquidStaking) or any asset whose fair value drifts from 1.0 bleeds LPs to arbitrage as the drift accumulates
findings.where: constructor L55-L56, _xp() L64-L67, docs L10-L13; consumer lst.sol exchangeRate() L63
findings.detail: The docs recommend this block for 'an LST against the asset it wraps'. The catalog's lst block is explicitly a wstETH-style share token whose exchangeRate() rises with rewards, not a rebasing 1:1 token. This pool has no rate oracle - the only multipliers are 10**(18-decimals) - so it will always centre its flat region at 1 share = 1 asset. Once exchangeRate is 1.02, the pool sells shares worth 1.02 for ~1.00 with only 4 bps of friction; arbitrageurs buy them until the pool is pushed far enough down the constant-product tail that the marginal price reaches 1.02, and they do it again on every reportRewards(). At A=200 that means LPs continuously hand the staking yield to arbitrageurs, hold a growing imbalance, and end up mostly in the asset. The same applies to any pair whose true ratio is not exactly 1 (a stable with a persistent discount, a wrapped token with a fee). Curve solves this with per-coin rate multipliers read from the LST (stored_rates) - the amplified region is then centred on the real exchange rate.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy ModLiquidStaking (shares) and a ModStableSwap(shares, asset) at A=200 as the docs suggest; LPs seed 10k/10k. 2. Operator calls reportRewards() over time; exchangeRate() goes from 1.00 to 1.02. 3. Arbitrageur: exchange(false, N asset) receiving ~N shares while the pool quotes near 1.00, then requestWithdrawal/claim at the LST for N*1.02 asset (or sells on any venue that prices shares correctly). 4. Repeat until the pool's marginal price reaches 1.02, which at A=200 requires the pool to be heavily skewed toward asset. 5. Every subsequent reward report repeats the extraction; LPs never receive the yield that the shares they hold are supposed to accrue.
findings.recommendation: Add per-coin rate hooks: an optional `rateProvider` per coin (e.g. the LST's exchangeRate()) multiplied into _xp() so the invariant is solved in underlying-asset units, as Curve's metapool/wstETH pools do. Until then, restrict the block to pairs whose fair ratio is 1.0 (fiat stables, PSM-backed stables, rebasing tokens - subject to STABLESWAP-6) and put this in the catalog help text; an LST-share pair belongs in ModAMM or in a pool with a rate oracle.

findings.title: Internal balance accounting with no sync/skim: fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens leave the pool insolvent or strand value
findings.where: addLiquidity() L135-L138, exchange() L171-L172 and L177-L178, removeLiquidity() L150-L158, collectAdminFees() L188-L196
findings.detail: balance0/balance1 are storage counters incremented by the requested amount, never reconciled with coin.balanceOf(this). A fee-on-transfer token delivers less than `amountIn` while the pool books the full amount, so the pool quotes and pays out against tokens it does not hold; the shortfall is realised by whoever withdraws last (removeLiquidity or exchange push reverts with PUSH_FAILED). A negatively rebasing token has the same effect; a positively rebasing one (rebasing stETH, the very asset the docs allude to) accrues tokens that no function can distribute - LPs cannot withdraw them, collectAdminFees does not see them, and there is no skim(). Tokens sent directly to the contract are likewise stranded (which, on the plus side, is why a donation-based first-depositor inflation attack does not work here). Conditional on the token wired, but the catalog accepts any erc20 on both ports.
findings.exploit: 1. Wire a token with a 1% transfer fee as coin1; LPs seed 1M/1M (the pool books 1M coin1 but holds 990k). 2. Traders swap normally; the pool keeps quoting and paying out on the phantom 10k. 3. The last LP to removeLiquidity, or any trader whose output exceeds what is physically left, hits PUSH_FAILED and their funds are stuck until someone donates the difference. Rebasing variant: wire rebasing stETH as coin0; after positive rebases the contract holds more stETH than balance0 and no path can ever release the excess.
findings.recommendation: Measure deposits and swap inputs as `balanceOf(this)` deltas around the pull, and add an owner/anyone `skim()` that sends balanceOf(this) - (balance + adminBalance) to the fee sink (or credits it to LPs). Document that rebasing and fee-on-transfer tokens are unsupported; for a rebasing LST wrap it first (the catalog's lst block already is a non-rebasing share token, see STABLESWAP-5).

findings.title: No deadline on any mutator and no minimum amounts on removeLiquidity
findings.where: addLiquidity() L127, removeLiquidity() L150, exchange() L162
findings.detail: exchange() has minOut and addLiquidity() has minShares, but nothing takes a deadline, so a transaction that sits in the mempool through a repricing (a de-peg, a setParams A change, a large flow) executes later at whatever the pool state has become, bounded only by the min the user chose at signing time. removeLiquidity() has no bounds at all: the caller gets a proportional cut of whatever the balances are when it lands, so an LP withdrawing during a de-peg or right after an attacker skews the pool receives a different mix than they quoted, with no way to say no.
findings.exploit: 1. LP signs removeLiquidity(shares) expecting ~50/50 of a 1M/1M pool. 2. Before it mines, a large exchange (or the STABLESWAP-1 flash push) skews the pool to 1.9M/0.1M. 3. The LP receives 95% coin0 / 5% coin1; if coin0 is the asset that is de-pegging, the LP has been forced to take the bad side. Deadline variant: a swap signed with a generous minOut mines a day later after an A change, filling at a price the user never intended.
findings.recommendation: Add `uint256 deadline` (require(block.timestamp <= deadline)) to addLiquidity, removeLiquidity and exchange, and `minAmount0, minAmount1` to removeLiquidity. Wallet UIs in the desk should populate them by default.

findings.title: adminFeeBps starts at 50% and is not a catalog parameter; collectAdminFees is permissionless and pays the owner when no sink is wired, so a renounced owner strands admin fees
findings.where: constructor L59, collectAdminFees() L188-L196, setFeeSink() L198-L200, setParams() L202-L208
findings.detail: Half of every swap fee is diverted from LPs to the protocol from the first trade, but the catalog exposes only amp_/feeBps_/name/symbol, so a deployer who reads the canvas thinks LPs earn the whole 4 bps. The owner can later set adminFeeBps to 10,000 (all fees) without a ramp or notice - bounded, but worth knowing when evaluating LP returns. collectAdminFees() can be called by anyone (fine) and pushes to feeSink or, if unset, to owner; if the deployer renounces via setOwner(address(0)) without wiring a sink, most tokens revert on transfer to address(0) and collectAdminFees reverts forever, stranding the admin balance (LP funds are unaffected since adminBalance is already excluded from balance0/1). The `sink` port wires setFeeSink post-deploy, so there is a window between construction and wiring where fees accrue to the owner address.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy with defaults and no feeSink. 2. setOwner(address(0)) to 'decentralise'. 3. Any later collectAdminFees() reverts (PUSH_FAILED on transfer to 0); adminBalance0/1 grow forever and can never be withdrawn.
findings.recommendation: Expose adminFeeBps_ as a catalog param (default 0 or 5000, stated), emit events on setParams/setFeeSink, and have collectAdminFees revert clearly (or skip) when the destination is address(0). Consider capping adminFeeBps changes or routing them through the governor port.

findings.title: Newton loops never revert on non-convergence, first deposit must be two-sided (Panic 0x12 otherwise), decimals above 18 revert the constructor
findings.where: getD() L71-L83, getY() L86-L97, addLiquidity() L133 and L141, constructor L55-L56
findings.detail: Unlike Curve, getD/getY return the last iterate after 255 rounds instead of reverting. Simulated: integer oscillation of a few wei prevents the <=1 tolerance from being met at balance skews above ~1e5:1 (and for A=1 above ~1e4:1), so the full 255 rounds run (roughly 100k extra gas), but the returned D matches a 60-digit reference to ~1e-28 relative error, so there is no pricing error and no DoS - just gas. The formulas match the reference implementation (ann = A*N, c = D^3/(x*N*ann*N), b = x + D/ann, out = x - y - 1 rounding against the trader) and a 3,000-case random sweep of getDy found no underflow in `2*y + b - d` or in `x - y - 1`; a dust trade returns (0,0) rather than reverting. getD divides by x0*N and x1*N, so the very first addLiquidity must supply both coins or the call reverts with a division-by-zero panic instead of a readable message; after that neither balance can reach zero through exchange (out < x). `10 ** (18 - decimals())` reverts for any coin with more than 18 decimals, and the coin must implement decimals().
findings.exploit: 1. First LP calls addLiquidity(1e18, 0, 0) -> Panic(0x12) with no revert string. 2. Or: wire a 24-decimal token as coin1 -> constructor reverts and the deployment plan fails after the upstream token has already been deployed.
findings.recommendation: Add `require(amount0 > 0 && amount1 > 0, "BOTH_COINS")` on the first deposit, `require(decimals <= 18)` in the constructor with a message, and either revert on non-convergence like the reference or document that the loop is bounded and accurate. Consider a smaller iteration cap (Curve's D converges in <20 rounds in all practical states).

safe_use: Never wire this block's `oracle` output into ModCDP, ModLendingPool, ModPerps or ModBonding. price() is manipulable spot: use ModFixedOracle or an external feed for anything that lends, mints or liquidates. If you must read the pool price off-chain, treat it as informational and note it is net of the swap fee and quoted as coin0 in coin1.

Pair only plain ERC20s whose fair ratio is exactly 1.0 (fiat stables, a PSM-backed stable against its reserve, MODUSD/USDC). Do not pair the catalog's lst shares with their asset here - the share price drifts above 1 and the pool has no rate provider; use ModAMM for that pair until rate hooks exist.
Do not wire fee-on-transfer, rebasing, or hook-bearing (ERC777/ERC1363) tokens. The pool books requested amounts, never reconciles with balanceOf, has no skim(), and has no reentrancy guard.

Wire the `governor` port to a ModTimelock/ModGovernor before adding liquidity so setParams (A, fees, admin share) is public and delayed; never change A in one step on a skewed pool - move it in small increments over days, and expect the price/virtualPrice to step each time.
Seed the first deposit with BOTH coins in the intended ratio (a one-sided first deposit reverts with a bare Panic). Both coins must expose decimals() <= 18.

Know that adminFeeBps starts at 50% of the swap fee and is not shown on the canvas; wire the `feeSink` port (or leave the owner as the recipient) before renouncing ownership, otherwise admin fees are stranded forever.

Pass tight minShares/minOut from the client and be aware there is no deadline and removeLiquidity has no minimum amounts - withdraw when the pool is near par, not during a de-peg, and prefer private/flashbots submission for large withdrawals.
Because deposits carry no imbalance fee, expect informed flow to route swaps through addLiquidity+removeLiquidity; size the LP return expectation on the assumption that only naive volume pays feeBps.
virtualPrice() is safe as an LP accounting number only while A is fixed: it is monotone under swaps and liquidity operations, but a setParams A change steps it in either direction.
